text: To incorporate something is to make it part of a bigger whole, so it stops being a separate thing and simply belongs. You can incorporate an idea into an essay or a new player into a team. Here the point is that walking slots into a day you were already having, instead of needing an hour of its own.

Something premature happens before the proper or usual time. The word is pre-, meaning before, plus mature, meaning fully grown or ready, so it is literally before-ready. A premature baby is born weeks early. Premature death here means dying earlier than you otherwise would have, not death in general.

To taper is to get narrower toward one end, the way a carrot or a candle does. From that shape the word also came to mean getting smaller and smaller in amount. When the benefits of walking taper off, each extra thousand steps still helps, but less than the thousand before it did.

Hippocrates was a Greek doctor who lived about 2,400 years ago and is often called the father of medicine, because he treated illness as something with natural causes worth studying rather than a punishment from the gods. Doctors today still swear a promise named after him. The article quotes a famous line about walking that people attribute to him, then admits nobody is sure he said it.

A physician is a doctor, and specifically one who treats illness with medicines and advice rather than by operating on you; a doctor who operates is a surgeon. It is the more formal word and turns up far more in writing than in speech. Hippocrates is introduced here as an ancient Greek physician.

Saying or so the story goes is a quick way of passing something on while making clear you cannot vouch for it. It signals that this is what people repeat, not something anyone has checked. The writer uses it because the famous walking quote may never have come from Hippocrates at all.

To dispute something is to argue that it is not true or not fair, so a disputed fact is one people still disagree about. You might hear of a disputed goal in football or a disputed border between countries. Whether Hippocrates really said that line about walking is disputed, meaning the experts cannot agree.

If something originated somewhere, that is where it began. The word is a relative of origin, the starting point of a thing. The question here is whether the phrase about walking originated with Hippocrates, that is, whether he was the first person to say it.

A kernel is the small seed or grain inside a shell, like a kernel of corn. Saying something contains a kernel of truth means that even if most of it is wrong or exaggerated, there is a small true bit at the centre. The quote may not really be Hippocrates's, but walking genuinely is good for you.

Unlock usually means to open something with a key, but it is often used for reaching a benefit that was there all along and out of reach. Video games borrow it this way when you unlock a new level. Here the question is how much walking it takes to unlock the health benefits.

Conventional wisdom is what most people take for granted as true, usually because they have heard it repeated rather than because anyone checked. Conventional means usual or standard. The conventional wisdom that you need 10,000 steps a day is exactly what this article sets out to test.

A target is normally the thing you aim at, but it is also used for a number you are trying to reach, like a savings target or a reading target at school. Nothing is being shot at. Here 10,000 steps is treated as a daily target.

Something questionable is doubtful, worth raising questions about. It does not mean definitely wrong, only that it should not be trusted without a second look. The writer says the source of the 10,000-step number is as questionable as the Hippocrates quote.

The origins of something are where and how it began. The word comes up most often with things whose beginnings are surprising or murky. The origins of the 10,000-step goal lie in advertising rather than in science.

A clinical trial is a carefully planned test of a treatment on real people, usually comparing a group that gets it with a similar group that does not, so the difference can be measured. New medicines have to pass trials like this before anyone is allowed to sell them. The writer's point is that the 10,000-step number never came from one.

A campaign is a planned series of actions aimed at one goal, run over weeks or months rather than in one go. There are election campaigns, charity campaigns and advertising campaigns. The 10,000-step idea came out of an advertising campaign, a stretch of ads all pushing the same product.

Launch means to send something off on its way, as with a rocket or a boat sliding into the water. Businesses use it for putting a new product on sale for the first time. The pedometer was launched before the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, meaning that is when it first went on sale.

A pedometer is a small device that counts your steps, clipped to a belt or pocket; ped- comes from the Latin for foot and -meter means measurer. Older ones worked with a little weight that swung and clicked once per step. The phone or watch that counts your steps today does the same job with sensors.

Kanji are the Chinese characters used in Japanese writing, where one character stands for a whole word or idea rather than a sound. Japanese uses them alongside two sound-based alphabets of its own. The article notes that the kanji for 10,000 looks a little like a walking person, which helped the advertisement along.

To be committed to something is to be firmly devoted to it and willing to keep at it. It is the same word used for making a promise you mean to keep. People committed to getting their steps in are the ones who take the daily goal seriously.

To shy away from something is to avoid it because it makes you uneasy, the way a startled horse shies sideways. It suggests hesitating rather than refusing outright. The writer says people fond of the 10,000 goal need not shy away from it, meaning there is no harm in keeping it.

A mark is usually something you write or a stain you leave, but it also means a particular level or point on a scale: the halfway mark, the one-mile mark. Here the 10,000 mark simply means the figure of 10,000 steps.

In terms of introduces the angle you are judging something by, as in cheap in terms of price but slow in terms of speed. It is a tidier way of saying when it comes to. The number is popular, but in terms of scientific research it has almost nothing behind it.

To have a leg to stand on is to have some support for your argument; without one, your case falls over the moment anybody pushes. It is nearly always used in the negative. Saying the 10,000-step number barely has a leg to stand on means there is hardly any evidence for it, and the writer is enjoying the pun about walking.

Lancet Public Health is a scientific journal, a publication that prints new research rather than news or stories. It belongs to the Lancet family, among the most respected names in medicine. A study appearing there has been read over by other scientists first, which is part of why this article trusts it.

Perambulation is a deliberately grand word for walking about: per- means through and ambulare is Latin for to walk. Hardly anyone says it out loud, and the writer is being playful by calling the research perambulation papers. The ordinary word would just be walking.

Papers here does not mean sheets to write on. In science a paper is a written report of one piece of research, published so that other scientists can read it, check it and build on it. Fifty-seven papers means fifty-seven separate published studies about walking.

To assess something is to look at it carefully in order to judge how big, how good or how serious it is. A teacher assesses your work; a doctor assesses an injury. This study set out to assess the connection between how much people walk and how healthy they turn out to be.

An outcome is how something turns out, so health outcomes are the health results researchers measure at the end: who fell ill, who recovered, who died and when. Scientists like the phrase because it covers all those different endings at once. Walking more improved nearly every health outcome this study looked at.
Beneficial means good for you, doing some real good. It is the adjective that belongs with benefit. Walking more turned out to be beneficial whichever health measure the researchers checked.

Across the board means for everything or everyone in a group, with no exceptions. The image comes from a betting board where you bet on every outcome at once. Walking more was beneficial across the board, meaning it helped with every illness measured, not just one of them.

In contrast to sets two things side by side to show how different they are. A contrast is a sharp difference, the way black looks against white. Seven thousand steps in contrast to two thousand means the researchers were comparing those two groups directly.

In everyday speech a risk is a chance of something bad happening. Scientists use it as a measurement: how often something happens in a group, which lets them compare one group against another. A 47 per cent lower risk of early death means early death happened 47 per cent less often among the people who walked more, not that any one walker has a 47 per cent chance of anything.

Cardiovascular disease covers illnesses of the heart and of the blood vessels: cardio means heart and vascular means the tubes that carry blood. Heart attacks and strokes are the best-known kinds, and together they kill more people worldwide than anything else. Walking 7,000 steps a day went with a 25 per cent lower chance of developing it.

Diabetes is a long-term illness in which the body cannot keep the amount of sugar in the blood under control, because it either makes too little insulin or has stopped responding to it properly. Left untreated, that damages eyes, nerves, kidneys and the heart. The common adult form is closely tied to how much people move, which is why a walking study measures it.

t: a little goes a long way
text: Saying a little goes a long way means a small amount achieves far more than you would expect, so you do not need much of it. People say it about strong spices and about kindness. Here it means even a small increase in walking, from 2,000 steps to 4,000, brings a surprisingly large improvement.

Mortality means death, and in research it means how much death happens in a group of people. It comes from the Latin for liable to die, which also gives us mortal. Mortality risk is a researcher's way of saying the chance of dying within the stretch of time being studied.

To track something is to follow it as it moves or changes, the way you follow an animal by its tracks or a parcel on its way to you. Researchers track people by checking on them again and again over years. This study tracked tens of thousands of walkers for about eight years.

To diminish is to get smaller, and a return is what you get back from an effort. Diminishing returns describes a situation where each extra bit of effort gives you less than the bit before it did: the first hour of revision helps a lot, the fifth hardly at all. Walking shows it plainly, because going from 2,000 steps to 4,000 helps far more than going from 7,000 to 10,000.

Return on investment is a business phrase for how much you get back compared with what you put in: the investment is what goes in and the return is what comes out. Scientists borrow it for effort of any kind. Dr Ding applies it to steps, because past about 7,000 you are putting in more walking and getting very little back.

An epidemiologist studies patterns of health and illness across whole populations instead of treating one patient at a time, asking who gets ill, where, and why. The word is a relative of epidemic. Their tools are numbers and comparisons between large groups, which is exactly what this walking study is built from.

Monash University is a large research university in Melbourne, in Australia. Universities do not only teach: a great deal of the research behind health news is done inside them. Both scientists quoted here work at Australian universities, Dr Ding in Sydney and Dr Stamatakis in Melbourne.

Scarcely means hardly or barely, only just enough to count. It belongs with scarce, meaning there is very little of something about. Saying extra steps beyond 7,000 are scarcely worth the effort means they do still help, but so little that you would hardly notice.

A jump is not always something you do with your legs. It also means a sudden increase from one number to a bigger one, as in a jump in prices or a jump in temperature. The jump from 7,000 daily steps to 10,000 is simply the increase between those two amounts.

Measure is usually a verb, but as a noun a measure is one particular way of putting a number on something. Height and weight are two different measures of a body. Step count is only one measure of walking; how fast you go is another.

Intensity is how strong or hard something is, as opposed to how much of it there is or how long it goes on. A short sprint has high intensity; a slow stroll has low intensity. In exercise, intensity is usually judged by how hard your heart and lungs are having to work.

To quantify something is to turn it into a number so it can be measured and compared; quantity means amount. Scientists have to quantify vague-sounding things all the time. Here they quantify how intense a walk is by counting steps per minute.

Cadence is the rate at which something repeats in a steady rhythm. Cyclists, runners and walkers use it for the number of steps or pedal turns per minute, and in music it describes the beat. The article gives 100 steps a minute as a brisk walking cadence.

An ideal version of something is the best possible one, the one you would choose if you could have anything. As a noun, an ideal is a standard to aim at. Scientists are still hunting for the ideal walking cadence, because the evidence does not yet point clearly at one number.

To pin something down is to fix it in place so it cannot shift, like pinning paper to a board; used about facts, it means getting an exact answer instead of a vague one. Things that keep slipping are hard to pin down. The best cadence is hard to pin down because different studies point at different numbers.

Sports science is the study of what exercise does to the body, drawing on biology, physics and medicine. It is why teams employ staff who measure heart rates and plan recovery, rather than simply telling players to train harder. Here it supplies the general rule that harder exercise tends to do more good.

Your heart rate is the number of times your heart beats in a minute, which you can count as a pulse at your wrist or neck. Resting, a child's might be 70 or 80; hard exercise pushes it far higher, because working muscles need blood delivered faster. Getting your heart rate up is a simple sign that exercise is actually asking something of you.

To be out of breath is to be breathing fast and hard after effort, too hard to talk comfortably. It happens because working muscles need more oxygen than calm breathing can deliver. Being a little out of breath is used here as a rough test that you are walking fast enough for it to count.

To align things is to line them up so they point the same way. Used about ideas, if one finding aligns with another then the two agree and point to the same conclusion. Dr Ding's view about intensity aligns with what the second study found.

The findings of a study are what the researchers found out: the results, stated plainly. Scientists prefer the word to proof, because a study reports what it saw rather than settling a question forever. The findings here are that both how much and how fast you walk matter.

The British Journal of Sports Medicine is another scientific journal, this one specialising in exercise, injury and sport. Journals are where research gets published once other experts have looked it over. The second study in this article appeared there in September.

Your colleagues are the people you work alongside, especially in a job that takes training. Modern science is nearly always done by teams, so a paper usually carries several names. Dr Stamatakis and his colleagues shared the work of following tens of thousands of people for eight years.

A joint is a place where two things meet, like your knee or elbow, but as an adjective joint means shared or combined: a joint effort, a joint decision. The researchers studied the joint effects of step count and speed, meaning the two of them working together rather than each on its own.

To participate is to take part, so participants are the people taking part in something, here in a study. Researchers use the word rather than subjects to make clear that the people agreed to join. This study had 64,743 participants, roughly the crowd in a big football stadium.

UK Biobank is a huge British research project that has gathered health information from half a million volunteers and keeps following them decade after decade. Scientists anywhere can apply to use it, which saves them having to recruit people themselves. Both the size of this study and its eight years of follow-up come from that store of information.

Data means recorded facts and figures, and a data set is one organised collection of them, gathered and kept together so it can be analysed. A spreadsheet of your class's heights is a tiny data set. A large one like UK Biobank lets researchers spot patterns far too faint to see in a small group.

Brisk means quick and energetic. A brisk walk is the pace you use when you are slightly late: fast enough to warm you up and to make talking a little harder. The word also goes with business and with weather, where brisk means sharp and fresh.

To amble is to walk slowly and without hurry, the way you drift around a shop with nowhere to be. It is the opposite of a brisk walk. The study found that 5,000 brisk steps did about as much good as 7,500 ambled ones, which is the whole point about speed.

An average squeezes a pile of different numbers into one typical value, found by adding them up and dividing by how many there were. Saying something holds on average means it is true of the group as a whole, while individuals land either side of it. On average the brisk walkers did as well as the slower ones who went further.

The sweet spot is the point where something works best, named after the place on a bat or racket where the ball flies off cleanly. Too little and too much are both worse than the spot in between. The paper puts the walking sweet spot at 7,500 to 10,000 steps a day with bursts of brisk walking.

An interval is a gap, or a stretch of time between two points, which is why the break in the middle of a play is called the interval. In exercise, intervals are short bursts of harder effort with easier stretches in between. The advice here is frequent intervals at 100 steps a minute rather than one long march.

Your pace is the speed you are moving at, and a pace is also a single step, which is where the meaning came from. Upping the pace means going faster. For people who cannot walk far, the article suggests walking faster as a way to get more out of the distance they can manage.

A sprint is a short run at full speed, the opposite of a long steady jog. Used loosely it means any brief burst of fast movement. The last line suggests parking a block away and doing a walking sprint to the shop, a stretch of deliberately fast walking.
